title: Who do you say I am (Mark 8:27–38)
hookLine: Peter gets the answer right and the meaning wrong

lines: WHAT DO PEOPLE SAY ABOUT ME?
ON THE ROAD TO CAESAREA PHILIPPI.
cards: What are people saying about me? From a friend, it's usually a nervous question. Today Jesus asks it, and he doesn't sound nervous.
He's walking with his disciples on the road to the villages of Caesarea Philippi, in the north, and he asks: who do people say I am? The answers come fast. John the Baptist, back from the dead.
Elijah. One of the prophets. Then he turns the question around, and there's nowhere to hide from it.

teach.b: First, the right answer. In the Douay-Rheims: "But whom do you say that I am? Peter answering said to him: Thou art the Christ." Christ isn't a last name.
It's a title, the Greek for anointed, and John's Gospel matches it to the Hebrew: "the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ." Israel's kings were anointed with oil.
Some readers call this the hinge of Mark's Gospel: near the middle, a disciple finally says it out loud. Second, the wrong meaning.

teach.h: THE SON OF MAN MUST SUFFER.
teach.b: Right away Jesus starts teaching, openly, Mark says, that the Son of man must suffer many things, be rejected, be killed, and rise again after three days. Peter takes him aside and rebukes him.
In Peter's picture, it seems, the Christ doesn't die.

teach.h: GO BEHIND ME: A DISCIPLE'S PLACE.
teach.b: Third, the rebuke back, and it's sharp: "Go behind me, Satan, because thou savourest not the things that are of God, but that are of men." Some readers dwell on the opening words. Go behind me: where a disciple walks.
Peter has stepped in front, trying to lead, and Jesus sends him back to his place. Fourth, the invitation to everyone.

teach.h: TAKE UP YOUR CROSS AND FOLLOW.
teach.b: Jesus calls the crowd over too: "If any man will follow me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me."

teach.h: WHOM DO YOU SAY THAT I AM?
teach.b: In Rome's world a cross wasn't jewelry. It was an execution, carried out in public, and Mark's own story will end at one.
Catholics read it as the shape of the whole Christian life: not a grim road, but following someone who walked it first.

how: Catholics profess who Jesus is each Sunday in the Creed, and Catholic devotion speaks of daily hardships as crosses carried with Christ, sometimes offering them up in prayer.

o: Jesus's family name, passed down from Joseph
a word meaning teacher, like rabbi
a title meaning anointed, like Messiah

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: John, Elijah, one of the prophets
the place where a disciple walks

s: it's a title: Greek for anointed, the same as the Hebrew Messiah.
Peter rebukes Jesus right after calling him the Christ
when Jesus speaks of suffering and death, Peter takes him aside and rebukes him.
in Jesus's world, a cross was a small daily annoyance
it was a Roman execution, carried out in public.

games.q: you're Peter. you've just said he's the Christ, and now he says he must suffer and be killed. what do you do?
o: take him aside and tell him that can't happen.
tell the crowd what he said.
games.why: Peter takes him aside and rebukes him, and hears, "Go behind me, Satan." the right answer, the wrong meaning.

practice: Imagine the road, the dust, and the question turned toward you: not what the Church says, not what your parents said, but who do you say he is?

Maybe the answer is sure, maybe it's I don't know yet, maybe it's a question back; any honest sentence counts, so say it quietly, once, and sit with it. If you pray, you can offer that sentence as your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Christ. Not a last name but a title, Greek for anointed: what Peter calls Jesus at Caesarea Philippi, and the hinge of Mark's Gospel. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: cross, the Roman stake of execution. take up your cross.

carryVoice: Your line: take up your cross. Peter had the name right; the road was the hard part. Two hundred fourteen days in.
